evals.prompt: Worker nodes in my EKS cluster 'EKS-Cluster' in us-west-2 aren't joining — I'm seeing a node that won't reach Ready. Diagnose why.
evals.expected_output: The agent calls read-only AWS APIs against EKS-Cluster, works the NJ node-join checklist, and produces a diagnostic report whose rows are labeled with NJ check identifiers and per-row Critical/High/Medium severities, identifies the blocker, and gives prioritized remediation. The structured NJ-ID + severity report format is what distinguishes the skilled run from a generic troubleshooting answer.

assertions.text: The report labels its checks with NJ identifiers (NJ1–NJ64), not just prose findings
Findings carry explicit Critical/High/Medium severity labels

assertions: The response is structured as the skill's node-join diagnostic report (per-check PASS/FAIL/SKIPPED status with evidence and fix), rather than a free-form list of possible causes
The diagnosis is scoped to node-join / node-readiness checks the skill defines (IAM/auth, security groups, VPC/DNS, bootstrap, AMI, compute source) rather than general cluster troubleshooting
The remediation steps are ordered by the severity of the blocking check

evals.prompt: A node in my EKS cluster 'EKS-Cluster' in us-west-2 is stuck NotReady and I'm not sure it's healthy. Can you diagnose what's wrong with the node?
evals.expected_output: The agent inspects EKS-Cluster via read-only APIs and explicitly determines whether the stuck node is a failed-to-join node versus a node that previously joined and then lost its backing instance/capacity, citing the specific evidence (e.g. node condition, backing-instance state, compute source) and naming the relevant NJ checks. It also names its node-side blind spot and points to the aws-eks-node-diagnostics-mcp complement for SSM-level confirmation.
assertions: The agent explicitly classifies the node as 'joined-then-lost / unhealthy' rather than 'never joined / bootstrap failure', and justifies that classification from the evidence it collected

assertions.text: The agent ties its reasoning to specific NJ check identifiers

assertions: The agent names the node-side blind spot and points to the aws-eks-node-diagnostics-mcp (SSM-based) complement for confirmation it cannot do from the API side

assertions.text: The agent does not claim to have performed a mutating or write operation

evals.prompt: My new EKS node group won't start after I upgraded the cluster to 1.33 — nodes fail with NodeCreationFailure and never join. The old 1.32 node group is fine. We use an AL2 AMI. Diagnose why the nodes won't join.
evals.expected_output: Diagnoses this as the AL2-on-1.33 blocker (NJ22): EKS-optimized AL2 AMIs were not published for 1.33+ (1.32 was the last), so an AL2 node group on 1.33 cannot launch. Flags it Critical, recommends migrating to AL2023 or Bottlerocket, and notes the AL2023 bootstrap change to nodeadm (NodeConfig/MIME) rather than bootstrap.sh.

assertions.text: Attributes the failure to the specific NJ22 AL2-on-1.33+ check
Flags the blocker at Critical severity using the skill's severity label

assertions: States the precise reason an AL2 node group cannot launch on 1.33: EKS stopped publishing AL2 AMIs and 1.32 was the last version to receive them (not merely 'AL2 is old' or a generic compatibility warning)
Notes the AL2023 bootstrap format change to nodeadm / NodeConfig MIME, which a generic AL2023 recommendation would omit

evals.prompt: My nodes get 'Unauthorized' and won't join. The node role ARN is arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/teams/platform/eks-node-role and I added that exact ARN to the aws-auth ConfigMap. Diagnose why the nodes still can't join.
evals.expected_output: Diagnoses the NJ7 aws-auth IAM-path gotcha: aws-auth does not accept a pathed role ARN, so the entry must have the path stripped to arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/eks-node-role. Flags it Critical and recommends migrating to EKS Access Entries, which handle paths correctly.

assertions.text: Attributes the failure to the specific NJ7 ARN-path check
Provides the exact path-stripped ARN as the fix

assertions: Explains that the fix is specific to aws-auth and does NOT apply to EKS Access Entries (which handle IAM paths correctly), and recommends migrating to Access Entries as the durable fix — the path-vs-Access-Entries distinction a generic answer would miss
